## Why Does Research Support Systematic Phonics?

The evidence base for systematic phonics instruction is one of the strongest in education research. The National Reading Panel’s 2000 meta-analysis reviewed 38 controlled studies and found that systematic phonics instruction produced significant benefits for students in kindergarten through sixth grade. The effect was strongest for younger children and for those at risk of reading difficulties.

Here are some of the key findings:

A 2006 review by Torgerson, Brooks, and Hall, published by the UK Department for Education, confirmed these results across international contexts. More recently, the 2023 report from the National Institutes of Health reaffirmed that explicit, systematic instruction in phonics and phonemic awareness produces the strongest outcomes for beginning readers.

The takeaway? Systematic phonics instruction is not a trend or a teaching preference. It is a research-backed approach supported by decades of evidence across multiple countries and student populations.

## Key Components of a Systematic Phonics Program

Not every phonics program qualifies as truly systematic. When evaluating a program for your school or classroom, look for these elements:

### A Defined Scope and Sequence

The program should have a clear, published order of skills. You should be able to look at the scope and sequence document and know exactly which phonics patterns students learn in Week 1, Week 10, and Week 30. A [well-designed scope and sequence](https://pridereadingprogram.com/structured-literacy-scope-sequence/) moves from the most common and regular patterns to less common and irregular ones.

### Explicit Instruction

Systematic phonics works best when paired with explicit teaching. This means the teacher directly models each skill, explains how it works, and guides students through practice before asking them to apply the skill independently. You might recognize this as the “I do, we do, you do” model. Students should never have to guess at patterns or figure them out on their own.

### Cumulative Review

Strong programs revisit previously taught skills regularly. If a student learned short vowel CVC words three weeks ago, those patterns should still show up in current lessons through decodable texts and practice activities. Cumulative review prevents the “learn it and forget it” cycle that undermines many reading programs.

### Decodable Texts

Students need practice reading connected text that uses the patterns they have actually been taught. Decodable readers are controlled texts where the majority of words follow phonics patterns students have already learned. This gives students real success experiences rather than forcing them to rely on guessing, picture clues, or memorization.

### Assessment and Mastery Checks

A systematic program includes regular checkpoints. These can be quick formative assessments, mastery checks, or progress monitoring tools. The data helps teachers know when a student is ready to move forward and when reteaching is needed.

**[See how phonics-based programs use these components to build strong readers.](https://pridereadingprogram.com/phonics-based-reading-programs/)**

## Systematic vs. Incidental Phonics Instruction

Understanding the difference between systematic and incidental phonics instruction is important, because both involve teaching phonics, but they produce very different results.

| Feature | Systematic Phonics | Incidental Phonics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequence | Follows a predetermined scope and sequence | Skills taught as they come up in reading |
| Planning | Lessons are planned around specific skills | Phonics is addressed spontaneously |
| Mastery | Students demonstrate mastery before progressing | No formal mastery requirements |
| Coverage | All major phonics patterns are taught | Gaps in coverage are common |
| Student outcome | Stronger decoding and reading accuracy | Inconsistent skill development |

Incidental phonics, sometimes called embedded or opportunistic phonics, teaches letter-sound relationships only when they arise naturally during shared reading or other literacy activities. While it can supplement a structured program, research consistently shows that incidental phonics alone does not give students the thorough grounding they need, especially students who struggle with reading.

The National Reading Panel found that systematic phonics instruction produced statistically significant improvements over incidental phonics in both word reading and text comprehension. For students with [dyslexia or other reading difficulties](https://pridereadingprogram.com/dyslexia-and-systematic-phonics-instruction/), the gap between the two approaches is even wider.

## How Do You Implement Systematic Phonics in the Classroom?

Knowing the research is one thing. Putting it into practice is another. Here are strategies that work across grade levels and settings.

### Start with Assessment

Before jumping into instruction, find out what each student already knows. A quick phonics screener or placement assessment can identify which skills a student has mastered and where the gaps are. This prevents wasting time reteaching what students already know, and it ensures no foundational skills are skipped.

### Follow the Sequence

Once you know your starting point, teach the skills in order. Resist the urge to skip ahead to “more interesting” patterns. Each skill in a well-built scope and sequence is there for a reason, and skipping creates gaps that show up later as decoding breakdowns. For guidance on building or evaluating a phonics sequence, see this [guide to phonics instruction in the early grades](https://pridereadingprogram.com/phonics-instruction-for-kindergarten/).

### Use the Explicit Lesson Cycle

A typical explicit phonics lesson follows this structure:

This cycle typically fits within a 30-40 minute block, making it practical even in busy classroom schedules.

### Integrate Multisensory Techniques

Research on [structured literacy approaches like Orton-Gillingham](https://pridereadingprogram.com/structured-literacy-instruction-with-the-pride-reading-program/) shows that engaging multiple senses strengthens memory and decoding skills. Have students trace letters in sand while saying sounds, tap out phonemes on their arm, or use letter tiles to physically build and manipulate words. These techniques are especially effective for students who need more repetition to reach mastery.

### Match Reading Materials to Instruction

The texts students read during phonics time should align with the skills you have taught. If your class has covered short vowels and consonant blends but not long vowel patterns, their practice reading should contain primarily short vowel and blend words. Decodable texts are designed for exactly this purpose.

**[Learn how phonics connects to the other four components of effective reading instruction.](https://pridereadingprogram.com/five-components-reading-guide/)**

## What Does a Systematic Phonics Scope and Sequence Look Like?

While specific programs vary, a solid scope and sequence for systematic phonics instruction generally follows this progression across the early grades:

| Phase | Skills Covered | Typical Grade Level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 1 | Letter names, letter sounds, CVC words (cat, sit, hop) | Kindergarten |
| Phase 2 | Consonant blends, digraphs, CVCC/CCVC words | Late K to early 1st |
| Phase 3 | Long vowel patterns (CVCe, vowel teams) | 1st grade |
| Phase 4 | R-controlled vowels, diphthongs, variant vowels | Late 1st to 2nd grade |
| Phase 5 | Multisyllabic words, syllable types, morphology | 2nd to 3rd grade |
| Phase 6 | Advanced patterns, Greek/Latin roots, affixes | 3rd grade and beyond |

The key principle across every phase is that new skills build on previously taught ones. A student working in Phase 3 should be comfortable with all Phase 1 and Phase 2 patterns. If they are not, the program should include reteaching and additional practice rather than pushing forward.

Many [structured literacy intervention programs](https://pridereadingprogram.com/structured-literacy-interventions-guide/) follow a similar progression but with more built-in repetition and smaller instructional steps for students who need intensive support.

## Common Challenges and How to Address Them

Implementing systematic phonics instruction is straightforward in theory, but teachers often run into practical obstacles. Here is how to handle the most common ones.

### Mixed Skill Levels in One Classroom

Most classrooms have students at different phonics skill levels. Small group instruction is the most effective solution. Use your assessment data to group students by skill level and teach targeted phonics lessons to each group. While one group works with you, others can engage in independent practice, partner reading, or phonics-based centers.

### Students Who Are Not Making Progress

If a student is stuck, the first step is to check for gaps in earlier skills. Often, a student who struggles with long vowel patterns has not fully mastered short vowels. Go back, reteach, and rebuild. If progress stalls despite targeted reteaching, consider a more intensive intervention approach with smaller group sizes and more repetition.

### Pressure to Move Faster

Pacing guides and curriculum timelines can create pressure to push ahead before students are ready. Resist this. Moving on before mastery creates a shaky foundation that collapses under more complex reading tasks. It is better to slow down and ensure mastery than to cover every lesson on schedule while students fall behind.

### Balancing Phonics with Other Literacy Components

Systematic phonics instruction should not exist in isolation. It is most powerful when integrated into a balanced literacy block that also includes read-alouds for vocabulary and comprehension, writing instruction, and opportunities for students to read texts at their independent level. The [Science of Reading research](https://pridereadingprogram.com/science-of-reading-phonics/) supports this integrated model.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between systematic and explicit phonics instruction?

Systematic phonics refers to the order in which skills are taught. It means following a planned scope and sequence from simple to complex. Explicit phonics refers to the method of teaching. It means directly modeling and explaining each skill rather than expecting students to discover patterns on their own. The most effective reading instruction combines both: it is systematic in its sequence and explicit in its delivery.

### At what age should systematic phonics instruction begin?

Most reading researchers recommend starting systematic phonics instruction in kindergarten, after students have developed basic phonemic awareness skills like identifying beginning sounds and rhyming. For students who enter first or second grade without a solid phonics foundation, systematic instruction should begin immediately, regardless of age.

### Does systematic phonics instruction work for older struggling readers?

Yes. The National Reading Panel found positive effects for students through sixth grade. Older students who struggle with decoding often have gaps in foundational phonics skills. A systematic approach identifies and fills those gaps. The instruction may look different for older students (age-appropriate materials, faster pacing through known skills), but the principles remain the same.

### How is systematic phonics different from whole language?

Whole language emphasizes learning to read through exposure to literature, using context clues, pictures, and memorization to identify words. Systematic phonics teaches students the code that connects letters to sounds, giving them tools to decode any word, including unfamiliar ones. Research overwhelmingly favors systematic phonics for building accurate, independent readers.

### Can parents use systematic phonics instruction at home?

Absolutely. Many phonics programs are designed to be parent-friendly with scripted lessons that require no teaching background. Parents can follow the same scope and sequence used in schools, practice decodable reading with their child, and use simple multisensory activities to reinforce skills. The key is consistency and following the sequence rather than jumping between random skills.

## Building Stronger Readers with Systematic Phonics

Systematic phonics instruction gives students something that no amount of guessing, memorizing, or relying on context can provide: a reliable system for reading words. When students understand how the written code works, they can decode unfamiliar words, spell with accuracy, and build the fluency needed for strong reading comprehension.

Whether you teach kindergarten, work with struggling readers in upper elementary, or support your child at home, a structured, sequential approach to phonics instruction is one of the most impactful choices you can make.

# Should We Teach with Decodable Text?

[Back to Blog](https://www.shanahanonliteracy.com/blog)

[SUBSCRIBE TO BLOG](#subscribe-now)  [![Comments](https://www.shanahanonliteracy.com/public/_front/shanahan/img/png/comment.png) 42 Comments](#comment-section)

![Blog Banner](https://www.shanahanonliteracy.com/upload/blogs/633/large/Mensvoort,-Richard-van-(1972-...)-Lente.jpg)

01 June, 2024

***Blast from the Past:*** *First published August 25, 2018; updated June 1, 2024*

*This blog considered the value of decodable text. Since then, there has been more research on the issue, so I thought it a good time to update. There have been several thoughtful reviews of the empirical research over the years, and these reflect a great deal of consistency among the scientists who think deeply about this issue. None of them rules out the use of decodables, but none claims that their use improves reading achievement. Those who recommend a heavy and/or long-term dose of decodable text in beginning reading programs are not doing so based on the science of reading. I’ve updated this piece a great deal and beefed up the research references. You might want to go back to the original blog to see the 45 comments that it elicited, so here is that link:*

***Teacher question:***

*Please share your thinking as well as research referencing the occasional use of decodable texts for small group reading instruction in grades K-2.*

**Shanahan responds:**

This is still not a highly researched topic. There have been only a handful of investigations into the effectiveness of decodable texts since the 1980s. And, truth be told, this collection of studies is a bit of a mess; with little evident agreement as to what decodable text is, what it should be compared with, and what learning outcomes should be expected.

Research has done less to solve the problem — do decodable texts advantage early reading development? — and more to demonstrate how complicated even simple ideas can be. (This is typical in the social sciences. Research studies often force us to operationalize constructs and that sometimes exposes how squishy soft our thinking is).

First issue… what is decodable text? Originally, the term was used relatively, it suggested more a continuum than a category (Juel & Roper-Schneider, 1985): phonics-oriented decodable texts used a preponderance of “words where all letters followed their major sound patterns.” The contrast to this was the basal readers of the time that employed a lower proportion of such words. Words like *pet, big, nap,*and *dot*would fit the decodable definition, while words like *cow, pear,*and *come*would not.

How regular did the words have to be to merit designation as decodable? Doesn’t decodability change with learning? As children know more spelling/pronunciation patterns, then those less frequent patterns become decodable, too.

Some researchers have tried setting percentages of decodability, and others have shifted the definitions to consider what the children have been taught at a given point.

If we all define decodable text in different ways then no one can be very happy with the research. No matter what a study finds, it becomes possible to reject research results out of hand because that may not be “what I meant by decodable.”

In that first study (Juel & Roper-Schneider, 1985), first graders taught with decodable texts outperformed the others in word reading, nonsense word reading, and the ability to read words they had not previously encountered – well, at least this was true when tested in November and February. However, by end of year, there were no differences when it came to either decoding ability or overall reading achievement. It is also fair to point out that the decodable group received more explicit phonics instruction, too. In other words, this study was more intriguing than determinative.

Since then, there have been a handful of empirical studies into the effectiveness of decodables. Sometimes with positive results (a 14 lesson study found that students were more likely to try to decode words in text if they worked with decodables (Mesmer, 2005)), and other times this experience seemed to reduce the likelihood of fluent reading (Price-Mohr & Price, 2018), or seemed to have no effect at all (students who worked with texts 11% decodable and 85% decodable did equally well in learning to read (Jenkins, et al., 2004)).

There are now almost as many research reviews on this topic as there are primary studies. These reviews all draw pretty much the same conclusions (Adams, 2009; Bier, 2007; Birch, et al., 2022; Cheatham & Alor, 2012; Mesmer, 2001). They acknowledge that decodable texts encourage students to apply their phonics skills (though this seems only to be true for most kids during a brief time during grade one). They also conclude that it is most prudent to use both decodables and non-decodables.

Hammering home that latter point is a new meta-analysis that examined more than 90 studies of early reading interventions. These studies were divided into 4 groups: those that did not employ text at all, those that only used decodables, those that did not use decodables, and those that used a combination of both. The text regime that significantly outdistanced the others in terms of how well they nurtured decoding ability was the diet that included decodables along with other texts.

Of course, there are several studies and evaluations of phonics instruction in which the program under investigation included decodable text (look at the phonics studies synthesized in the National Reading Panel Report or the various reports of What Works Clearinghouse). These phonics programs have been successful, but there is no evidence that without decodables they would have been any less effective. Phonics programs with and without them both seem to do well.

There are still methodological problems that need to be worked out on the research end of this. Researchers have usually failed to control the effects of other text factors. For instance, the amount of word repetition and the frequency of the words in the various texts are important variables that may confound the results of these studies (Mesmer, Cunningham, & Hiebert, 2012).

Finally, English is complex, and the sounds associated with letters and letter combinations depend on the letter’s position in the syllables, morphology, and etymology. That’s why so much is made these days of “statistical learning.”

Readers start to discern that *b* is more often associated with the /b/ sound in words like *big* and *bad* much more often than it will serve as a silent letter (such as in words like *bomb*or *climb*), and they learn to respond to this statistical difference accordingly. If unsure of the pronunciation of a *b* word, go with /b/; you’re more likely to get it right. Presenting students with lots of decodable text, text that’s much more regular that normal text, might mess up some of these cognitive calculations. Dick Venezky and Dale Johnson (1973) long ago showed that adults attribute sounds to letters in proportions more reflective of their appearance in children’s primers than of the actual proportions in which they appear in English language overall. (This is a problem for both leveled readers and decodable texts.)

I think it’s okay to use decodable texts as part of phonics instruction, but such practice should be limited, and even beginning readers should be reading (not just listening to) more than decodable texts.

Cheatham, J. P., & Allor, J. H.  (2012). The influence of decodability in early reading text on reading achievement: A review of the evidence.*Reading and Writing: An Interdisciplinary Journal, 25*(9), 2223-2246*.* <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-011-9355-2>

Timothy Shanahan Jun 02, 2024 12:22 PM

Mat--  
 The trick to beginning reading books is that they have to be easy enough for kids to read -- and that means they usually have to have some intentional alteration of the language to support the kids (but not so much support that they get the wrong idea). Hyper decodability is one of those tools, so using decodables to give kids practice with the skills they are learning makes sense. However, if you overdo it with those texts (as is often recommended these days), then kids learn the alteration you have made which may cause them problems down the road. Another simplification is to use texts with high frequency words (words the students are very likely to have in their oral language -- so no barriers to understanding, but with high amounts of repetition, using those individual words over and over but in different contexts (not the repetitive sentence patterns of predictable books which discourage kids from looking at the words). There are a number of such easy readers (the beginning levels of the Pete the Cat books are an example) and for examples of texts that have both properties -- decodability and controlled vocabualry, I would suggest that you go to the Text Project website. Freddie Hiebert provides such texts for free (and at least some of hers have been used in her research). Those kinds of texts are also an alteration that can become a crutch for some kids but by using both kinds of texts you decrease the chances of kids learning the adjustment rather than how to read.  
   
 tim

Timothy Shanahan Jun 02, 2024 09:49 PM

Jacinta--  
   
 Sorry for the confusion. Decodable and undecodable are both misnomers. Decodability is not a discrete variable (yes/no, black/white, up/down), but a continuous one. Texts are manipulated for young readers to increase the degree of decodability. Supposedly, undecodable text may actually be quite decodable. The same can be said about vocabulary controls -- how much repetition is there? how many words only appear once or twice in a text? and so on. When studies claim a text is decodable they are either talking about the percentage of words that are spelled/pronounced in the most frequent way or about whether an instructional program had taught the skills needed to pronounce words with those spellings. Undecodable either means that no one manipulated the text to increase its decodability or it really means less decodable (we manipulated these passages to be 70% decodable while these were only 30% decodable by our definition). In any event, by any definition or measure, there is some evidence showing that students will be more likely to sound out words if they are asked to read decodables for a very short period of time -- lessons over 12 days in first grade, and no research showing an advantage when it comes to learning to read.   
   
 tim

Megan Harvey Aug 08, 2025 07:09 PM

It seems there is much sentiment in the reading community that we should NOT be leaving young readers alone with texts that contain words they haven't learned to decode/recognize yet. I just read a different post today that basically said if we teach phonics/decodables in the morning and do leveled readers/non-decodable texts in the afternoon (ie. use 3 cuing), we send our students a mixed message about how to address unknown words. I think there is value in mixing reading both early on. I actually came accross this article becuase I was searching out how and when to transition from decodables to non-decodables. My question is, how should early readers be taught to approach unknown words in non-decodable texts?

![](https://www.shanahanonliteracy.com/public/_front/shanahan/img/jpg/blog-inner-img.jpg)

Gwen Quinn Nov 30, 2025 12:29 AM

Dr. Shanahan, I need your help!  
   
 In designing comprehensive learning experiences for English learners (grade 3 and above) who are in need of learning code-based skills, I’m hesitant on suggesting that teachers use connected text or decodable texts due to the grade typically associated with those types of phonics skills. What is your advice on navigating teaching code-based skills and providing opportunity for ELs to apply those skills in texts? Obviously, I’m considering their L1 literacy abilities and if/how their L1 assists or doesn’t with the development of English. Also, I want to note that the majority of their (EL) ELA block is experiencing opportunities to listen, speak, read and write along side their English speaking peers. This dynamic provides for an abundance of oral language development. The code based skill instruction would be 20min in length. Should we be pulling in a grade level portion of text to provide the opportunity to see the skill in action or stick with the connected text that is part of the K-2 program?

![](https://www.shanahanonliteracy.com/public/_front/shanahan/img/jpg/blog-inner-img.jpg)

Timothy Shanahan Dec 11, 2025 08:44 PM

Gwen-  
 When teaching decoding skills, it makes sense to give kids practice applying those skills (as part of the phonics instruction). I would make that decodable reading part of those 20 minutes that you noted.

English for kids

LearnEnglish Kids is a fun, educational website for children aged 5-12 who are learning English. There are lots of songs, stories, videos, activities and grammar and vocabulary games to help children develop their literacy skills while having fun. The website also has resources for parents and teachers. Visit [LearnEnglish Kids](http://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/en/) or see below for an overview of the different sections of the website.

## English reading and writing

The LearnEnglish Kids website has lots of activities to help children practise their reading and writing in English and improve their vocabulary. Children can also create their own avatar, post comments and write messages to other children around the world in a safe online environment. Go to [LearnEnglish Kids Read and Write](https://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/read-write).

## Learn English with games for kids

Children can have fun playing games and learning English at the same time! We have lots of free online vocabulary and spelling games for girls and boys to play. There are games for children at nursery, kindergarten and primary school. Go to [Learn English with Kids Games](https://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/games).

## English speaking and spelling

Children can learn how to speak and spell English words with Sam and Pam, the super space spies. They can improve their English pronunciation through songs and stories, learn about spelling rules, practise their English spelling and play phonics games. Go to [LearnEnglish Kids Speak and Spell](https://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/speak-spell).

## Learn English with audio and video

Do your children like listening to stories and songs in English? In this section they can find lots of animated songs and cartoon stories. They can also practise their speaking with fun tongue twisters and watch videos of children telling us about their lives. Visit [LearnEnglish Kids Listen and Watch](https://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/listen-watch).

## Learn English for parents and teachers

LearnEnglish Kids is also for teachers and parents with hundreds of free printable resources. There is a support section for parents with a discussion forum and advice on how you can help your children learn English outside of the classroom. Teachers can use most of the activities on the site with their young learners. Visit [LearnEnglish Kids Parents](http://learnenglishkids.britishcouncil.org/en/parents) section.

## Premier Skills English

If you are learning English and are interested in football, Premier Skills English can help you improve your English while you learn about the Premier League clubs and players. You can also find out about the matches and the Premier League rules and play games and do quizzes. Go to [Premier Skills English](http://www.britishcouncil.org/premierskills).

# British Council releases an English Phonics App for Kids

[](https://www.britishcouncil.sg/about/press/english-phonics-app-kids)Tuesday 28 August 2012

Singapore– The British Council has released**LearnEnglish Kids: Phonics Stories**, an **interactive phonics-based story app for iPad**.LearnEnglish Kids: Phonics Stories is based on the UK phonics curriculum, ’Letters and Sounds’, and contains a collection of eight stories, each focusing on a different set of sounds.

### What is phonics?

Phonics is a way of teaching reading which helps children understand language they see by introducing letters by their sound rather than name. This encourages them to connect the words they see with the words they hear.

When we spell letters we usually use the names of individual letters. So we say the first three letters of the alphabet like this: ‘ay, bee, cee’. But it can be easier for children to start by learning the sounds letters make, for example the word ‘cat' is sounded ‘c-a-t' not ‘cee-ay-tee'.

There are 26 letters in the alphabet but phonics uses about 44 sounds that combine or ‘blend’ to make words in English. Students are also taught to recognise sounds made by combinations of letters such as ‘ch' and ‘sh'.

The idea is that children see letters or combinations of letters and they are able to say the sound the letters make. They can then put these sounds together to make words.

### Build literacy and speaking skills

The app takes full advantage of the iPad’s technical capabilities and features crisp, high-definition illustrations, read-along audio narration and hundreds of interactive flaps and buttons for an engaging and dynamic reading experience.

‘LearnEnglish Kids: Phonics Stories is an exciting addition to the suite of LearnEnglish apps which the British Council offers,’ says Tracy Dumais, Mobile Learning Consultant at the British Council. ‘We are very excited to offer a story-book app which helps build a foundation for early literacy and speaking skills, and at the same time enables and encourages real-time interaction between children and family members through reading. The addition of FamLoop to LearnEnglish Kids: Phonics Stories really creates a unique family reading experience.’

LearnEnglish Kids: Phonics Stories is the British Council’s second app for young learners. The mobile app offers one free story on download and seven other stories available for purchase at US$1.99 each. The first three paid stories are currently available and the others will be released thereafter.

The App includes parent’s guide in six languages: English, Cantonese, Thai, Korean, Japanese and Traditional Chinese, so parents are able to teach children using specific activities and exercises recommended by British Council.

## About this app

Learn English through fun, animated song and story videos. Safe, ad-free games and activities help your child develop in these key areas in English: reading, listening, speaking and grammar.  
   
Recommended ages: 6–11  
   
OVER 100 QUALITY VIDEOS   
Our animated songs and stories are created by the British Council’s language learning experts and grouped into themes like fairy tales, classic children’s songs and grammar chants. Each video comes with subtitles that can be turned on or off to help children read and listen. Download all the videos to watch them whenever you want, even offline!  
Videos include: Little Red Riding Hood, Goldilocks, Jack and the Beanstalk, Old MacDonald, The Wheels on the Bus, Incy Wincy Spider and the Tales of Shakespeare.  
   
A LISTEN-AND-RECORD ACTIVITY ENCOURAGES SPEAKING  
Each animated video comes with an engaging listen-and-record activity that encourages your child to say and repeat the words from the video, building confidence in speaking over time. Children can listen to the narrator, record themselves and compare their pronunciation with the narrator’s.  
   
GAMES TO IMPROVE SPELLING, UNDERSTANDING AND GRAMMAR  
Each pack of animated videos comes with challenging word, grammar and spelling games to help children learn and understand the language they see in the videos.  
  
FOLLOW YOUR CHILD’S PROGRESS  
In each pack you can see how your child is progressing in five areas: Videos, Speaking, Spelling, Understanding and Grammar.  
   
AVAILABLE IN MULTIPLE LANGUAGES  
The app is available in English, French, Simplified Chinese and Spanish. Go to the Parents’ area to change the language.  
   
SAFETY AND DATA PRIVACY  
Your child’s privacy is very important to us. The app provides a completely safe and ad-free learning environment. We do track how the app is used, such as which games/videos are most popular, but we only use this information to make the app better for your child. We do not collect any information about your child or your family.   
   
LearnEnglish Kids: Playtime SUBSCRIPTION:  
Subscribe to unlock UNLIMITED access to all songs, stories and games.  
One-month and six-month subscription periods available.   
Price of subscription will vary depending on plan selected and region.  
Payment is charged to Google Play account at confirmation of purchase.  
Your Google Play account will be charged at the same price for renewal within the 24-hour period prior to the end of the current payment period unless auto-renewal is turned off in your Google Play account settings.   
Manage your subscriptions or turn off subscriptions anytime by going into the Google Play account settings after purchase.  
Any unused portion of a free trial period, if offered, will be forfeited when the user purchases a subscription to that publication, where applicable.

# Phono StoryForge

License: Apache 2.0
Python 3.11+

License: Apache 2.0
Python 3.11+

Phono StoryForge is a closed-loop adaptive reading tutor for early and struggling readers (dyslexia-aware), built on Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK). It doesn't just generate a decodable storybook once — it keeps a per-child mastery model, decides what phonics skill to teach next from that child's own reading evidence, generates a book guaranteed decodable at exactly that level, listens to the child read it, attributes every miscue down to the specific grapheme, updates the mastery model, and lets the next book change because of how this read went. # Phono StoryForge

[![License: Apache 2.0](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/798509b4df525f56802b56f8096862487f08023e3d7561c68656f8dab10d0d6e/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f6c6963656e73652d4170616368652d2d322e302d626c75652e737667)](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/798509b4df525f56802b56f8096862487f08023e3d7561c68656f8dab10d0d6e/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f6c6963656e73652d4170616368652d2d322e302d626c75652e737667)

Phono StoryForge is a **closed-loop adaptive reading tutor** for early and struggling readers (dyslexia-aware), built on Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK). It doesn't just generate a decodable storybook once — it keeps a per-child mastery model, decides what phonics skill to teach next from that child's own reading evidence, generates a book guaranteed decodable at exactly that level, listens to the child read it, attributes every miscue down to the specific grapheme, updates the mastery model, and lets the *next* book change because of how this read went.

Built as the capstone project for Google/Kaggle's **5-Day AI Agents Intensive — Vibe Coding Capstone**, Track: **Agents for Good** (education).

## The Problem

Parents of dyslexic and struggling readers are told to "read decodable books at their level," but (1) decodable books at the *exact* combination of phonics level + interests + age a given child needs are scarce and generic, and (2) nothing adapts: there's no loop that watches what the child actually misreads and chooses what to practice next. Phono StoryForge closes that loop — content generation guaranteed decodable for *this* child, plus an evidence-driven tutor that targets their real gaps and adapts session over session.

## The thesis: a closed loop, not a one-shot generator

The spine of the project is one loop, run per child, per session:

Everything load-bearing here is **deterministic, non-LLM Python** that the project already implements and unit-tests:

| Step | Module | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan | `app/skills/planner.py` `select_objective` | Picks the lowest unmastered grapheme (ZPD) from the child's BKT estimate, plus spaced-review picks. |
| Decode/verify | `app/skills/decodability.py` `decompose` | The keystone: maps any word → ordered graphemes tagged by phonics level. Powers decodability, targeting, and miscue attribution from one source of truth. |
| Assess | `app/skills/alignment.py` `assess` | Aligns expected vs. spoken text (running-record miscue types), then attributes each error down to the exact grapheme → `grapheme_evidence`. |
| Update | `app/skills/mastery.py` `update_from_evidence` | 4-parameter Bayesian Knowledge Tracing; turns evidence into an updated per-grapheme knowledge state. |
| Persist | `app/store/` | `LearnerProfile` (current mastery) + append-only `SessionLog` history. |

## Evidence: adaptive beats a fixed sequence

`eval/experiments/adaptive_vs_static.py` runs two arms over the same paired, seeded simulated learners: **adaptive** (`select_objective` chooses each session's target from the child's BKT estimate) vs. **static** (a fixed scope-and-sequence that ignores the evidence). Both close the identical loop; both children read the same fixed benchmark probe each session so the fluency comparison is fair.

`eval/experiments/adaptive_vs_static.py`
`select_objective`

Result (n=30, 40 sessions): **probe accuracy +0.06, true mean latent mastery +0.04, +4.9 WCPM**. Fully deterministic and LLM-free, so it reproduces exactly. Chart + CSV under `eval/experiments/results/`.

`eval/experiments/results/`

**On rigor (Stage D, de-circularized).** Those numbers are from an *independent* learner whose generative process is deliberately **not** what the tutor assumes — so the experiment is no longer self-validating. Two mismatches were introduced (`eval/simulated_learner.py`): (1) **emission** is a logistic/IRT curve with per-grapheme item difficulty, not the linear slip/guess that BKT inverts — the tutor must estimate mastery under a model it cannot represent; (2) **learning has no prerequisite/ZPD gate** (the planner's own thesis) — skills are learned by direct practice and *forget* when unpracticed, so adaptive can only win by revisiting each child's decaying frontier. The gaps roughly halve versus the earlier self-consistent learner but stay positive, and the accuracy advantage holds across all 12 cells of a forgetting/discrimination sweep (`eval/experiments/robustness_sweep.py`; narrowing to +0.002 at the harshest corner) — a smaller, more credible win. One honest wrinkle: on the count of graphemes pushed past a hard 0.95 mastery bar, adaptive and static are a wash (the fixed drill over-concentrates practice), even though adaptive wins on real reading accuracy, mean mastery, and fluency.

[Skip to content](#content)


[![](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/logo-2.png)](https://www.opensourcephonics.org)



# Free Phonics Materials for Teachers, Tutors, and Families

Literacy is a civil right.The research supporting phonics is too strong to ignore.All families deserve access to high-quality phonics materials.

![](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/AdobeStock_431482486-1024x540.jpeg)

# Why Open Source Phonics?

Many third, fourth, and older-grade students need more practice in order to master the phonics patterns needed to sound out new words and read and write fluently. Commercial programs designed for struggling readers are hundreds of pages long and expensive. Thus, they are not shared with all the teachers, students, and families who could use them.

[Read more](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/why-open-source-phonics/)

# Phonics practice with Open Source Phonics materials is effective, fun, and hands-on.

![](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Screen-Shot-2021-07-05-at-1.52.23-PM-1024x674.png)

## [Locking In Patterns](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/sequence/)

Students learn phonics patterns, affixes, and spellings in a step-by-step way.  
 Oral sound play (which increases phonological awareness) and brainstorming (which increases phonological awareness and vocabulary) is fun. Students get multiple opportunities to read and write new patterns—no guessing involved.

![](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/AdobeStock_409579006-1024x682.jpeg)

## [Writing From Dictation](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/lessons/)

This is where the rubber hits the road. Students “own” the patterns that they can write from dictation. In each lesson, adults read sentences aloud for students to write on white boards. Writing helps reading, as students “lock in” patterns; plus, students expand what they can write and spell with confidence.

![](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/AdobeStock_414390709-1-scaled-e1630096373651-1024x830.jpeg)

## [Reading Aloud](https://www.opensourcephonics.org/decodable-stories/)

Students do “triple reads” of longer decodable stories while adults cheer them on. With repeated readings, students increase fluency, speed, and stamina. Without the “curve balls” of patterns they cannot yet decode, students experience the thrill of fluent reading—where  reading aloud feels more like talking. This practice prepares students to read real texts in school.

# Endorsements for Open Source Phonics

I whole-heartedly support initiatives such as this one which work to provide high quality literacy instructional materials to all teachers and readers. Decodable texts provide students the opportunity to apply the phonics patterns they have been taught in decoding words in context. Using context clues to “guess” unknown words and/or skipping unknown words are  
 unreliable strategies that are not supported by research. Skilled readers are able to use their knowledge of phonics (e.g., sound-symbol correspondences and patterns, orthographic syllable types, morphology, and syllable division patterns) to decode unknown words, rather than guess or skip. Decodable texts contain words with phonics patterns students have been taught so they can learn to utilize these skills proficiently, and over time move to less controlled and more authentic texts. I admire and applaud Katie Spurlock’s work to make decodable texts available to every teacher and reader with internet access. I have reviewed her phonics sequence, lessons, and initial set of decodables and confirm their alignment with evidence-based structured literacy instruction.  
 **Every** child deserves the best opportunity to learn to read, and this is one step in that direction.

EMILY CANTRELL Clinical Associate ProfessorTeaching, Learning, and Culture Texas A&M University

What a service to the world of reading instruction! It's comprehensive, clear, systematic, cumulative, and explicit. The lesson format is excellent: review, phoneme awareness, concept presentation, guided practice in both reading and writing to dictation. The scope and sequence is solid, as good as any phonics program out there. The quality and amount of decodable text practice is exceptional!! The selection, inclusion, and gradual teaching of more irregular words is very well done and the methods align with current understandings.

Dr. Louisa MoatsLiteracy Expert and Author of LETRS

# Free Decodable Texts for Each Phonics Skill

Looking for free decodable texts? Use the below list to match a decodable text with the spelling pattern you’re teaching. And if you're just getting started, be sure to check out our [How to Use Decodable Texts](https://readinguniverse.org/article/explore-teaching-topics/word-recognition/phonics/how-to-use-decodable-texts) article.

## Why Decodables?

In this video, Dr. Louisa Moats discusses why teachers should use decodables in their classrooms, and how to know when it’s time to move on.

![Video thumbnail for How Long Should Students Work with Decodable Text?](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/zuxq-jneGtQ/maxresdefault.jpg)

Hide Video Transcript Show Video Transcript

Decodable text is a necessary part of a phonics lesson. What's the point of learning the correspondence unless you can use it in reading? So it's to provide that practice. Many students need a lot of practice using what you've taught them in a phonics lesson. It's not often not great literature; it's not for that purpose. It's for providing practice and reinforcement. So how long does it need to go on? ... Until the student can use most of the regular correspondences to read words accurately, and the student has a sight vocabulary, if you will, of probably several thousand words. Students differ. Some students can make that transition more quickly than others. So you have to keep data on the accuracy of student reading with decodable text to be sure that they have internalized what they've been taught.

### List of Decodables by Skill

Reading Universe offers a free collection of 95+ decodable texts organized by phonics skill. Following the scope and sequence illustrated in our [word recognition continuum](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/word-recognition/word-recognition-continuum), you can use these decodables with whatever phonics curriculum your school is using.

### Short Vowels

* Short ‘a’: [Mac the Cat](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-mac-the-cat), [Val and the Rat](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-val-and-the-rat)
* Short ‘i’: [A Wig in the Pit](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-a-wig-in-the-pit), [A Rip in the Bag](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-a-rip-in-the-bag)
* Short ‘o’: [The Big Job](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-the-big-job), [The Hot Pot](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-the-hot-pot)
* Short ‘u’: [The Fun Gig](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-the-fun-gig), [A Box of Hats](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-a-box-of-hats)
* Short ‘e’: [The Red Hen](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-the-red-hen), [The Pen](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-the-pen)
* All short vowels: [Pals on the Bus](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-pals-on-the-bus), [Zed the Cat](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-zed-the-cat)

The **[short vowels skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/explore-teaching-topics/word-recognition/phonics/beginning-phonics-patterns/short-vowels-skill-explainer/an-overview-of-short-vowel-sounds)** has everything you need to teach this, including lesson plans, student practice activities, and videos of great classroom instruction.

### Glued Sounds

* Glued sound 'am': [Pam and Sam](https://readinguniverse.org/pdf/explore-teaching-topics/word-recognition/phonics/phonics-patterns/decodable-pam-and-sam)
* Glued sound 'an': [Tan and Me](https://readinguniverse.org/pdf/explore-teaching-topics/word-recognition/phonics/phonics-patterns/decodable-tan-and-me)
* Glued sound 'all': [A Big Ball,](https://readinguniverse.org/pdf/explore-teaching-topics/word-recognition/phonics/phonics-patterns/decodable-a-big-ball) [Hal and the Red Ball](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/flossz-pattern-skill-explainer/decodable-hal-and-the-red-ball)
* Glued sounds '-ang', '-ing', '-ong', and '-ung': [The Swing](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-swing)
* Glued sounds ‘-ank’, ‘ink’, and ‘-unk’: [The Bunk Bed](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-bunk-bed)

See the **[glued skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/glued-sounds-skill-explainer/overview-of-glued-sounds)** for more instructional resources.

### Open Syllables

* Open syllables: [Bo and Jo](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/decodable-text-bo-and-jo)

See the **[open syllables skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/open-syllables-skill-explainer/overview-of-open-syllables)** for more instructional resources.

### Digraphs

* Digraph ‘sh’: [The Posh Ship](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-posh-ship), [The Wish,](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/consonant-digraphs-skill-explainer/decodable-the-wish) [Josh and Pam Shop](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/consonant-digraphs-skill-explainer/decodable-josh-and-pam-shop)
* Digraph ‘ch’: [Lunch at the Fish Shack,](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-lunch-at-the-fish-shack) [Chums](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/consonant-digraphs-skill-explainer/decodable-text-chums)
* Digraph ‘th’: [One Big Bath](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-one-big-bath)
* Digraph ‘ck’: [Jack the Buck](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-jack-the-buck)
* Digraph ‘wh’: [Whit's Bad Luck](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-whits-bad-luck)

See the **[consonant digraphs skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/consonant-digraphs-skill-explainer/overview-of-consonant-digraphs)** for more instructional resources.

### Blends

* Ending blends: [The Bent Tent](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-bent-tent), [The Bunk Bed](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-bunk-bed), [The Swing](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-swing)
* Consonant blends: [Lunch at the Shack](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-lunch-at-the-shack)
* Beginning and ending blends: [The Lost Raft](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-lost-raft), [Clams at the Pond](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-clams-at-the-pond), [The Band](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/closed-syllables-skill-explainer-2/decodable-the-band)

See the **[blends skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/blends-skill-explainer/overview-what-are-blends)** for more instructional resources.

### '-ck' Spelling Rule

* '-ck' Spelling Rule: [Nick and Jim Must Get Back!](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/ck-pattern-skill-explainer/decodable-ck-spelling-rule-nick-and-jim-must-get-back)

See the [**'-ck' spelling rule skill explainer**](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/ck-pattern-skill-explainer/overview-of-the-ck-spelling-rule) for more instructional resources.

### FLoSS(Z) Spelling Rule (Double Consonant Endings)

* Double consonant ending patterns - ‘-ff,’ ‘-ll,’ ‘-ss,’ and ‘-zz’: [Buzz and the Quill](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/flossz-pattern-skill-explainer/decodable-buzz-and-the-quill)

See the **[FLoSS(Z) spelling rule skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/flossz-pattern-skill-explainer/overview-of-the-flossz-spelling-rule)** for more instructional resources.

### 'y' as a Vowel

* ‘y' as a vowel when it spells the long ‘i’, /ī/, sound: [Sky the Shy Cat (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/decodable-sky-the-shy-cat-reading-universe.pdf)
* ‘y' as a vowel when it spells the long ‘e’, /ē/, sound: [The Party for Bunny (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/decodable-the-party-for-bunny-reading-universe.pdf)

See the [**'y' as a vowel skill explainer**](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/y-as-a-vowel-skill-explainer/overview-of-y-as-a-vowel) for more instructional resources.

### Magic 'e' (also known as Silent ‘e’)

* [Magic ‘e’ Decodable Texts Collection (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/Decodables/decodable-texts-silent-e-reading-universe.pdf)

**One-Syllable Words with Magic ‘e’**

* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘o-e': [A Trip to the Home Store](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-a-trip-to-the-home-store)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘a-e’: [Jobs for Rose and Jake](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-jobs-for-rose-and-jake)
* Magic  ‘e’ pattern ‘i-e’: [Hike, Bike, Swim](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-hike-bike-swim)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘u-e’: [Twins](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-twins), [The Class Trip](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-class-trip)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern (all long vowels): [Planning a Trip](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-planning-a-trip), [The Pen Pal Project](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-pen-pal-project)

**Multisyllable Words with Magic ‘e’**

* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘o-e’: [The Sibling Squabble](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-sibling-squabble)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘a-e’: [The Math Problem](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-math-problem)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern  ‘i-e’: [The Homesick Pilot](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-homesick-pilot)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘u-e’: [Duke](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-duke)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern ‘e-e’: [The Stampede](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-stampede)
* Magic ‘e’ pattern (all long vowels): [The Extreme Race](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-extreme-race)

See the **[magic 'e' skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/magic-e-skill-explainer/overview-of-magic-e)** for more instructional resources.

### Soft ‘c’ and Soft ‘g’

* Soft 'c' and soft 'g': [A Fun Day for Grace, Ace, and Spice (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/decodable-a-fun-day-for-grace-ace-and-spice-reading-universe.pdf)
* Hard and soft 'c': [A Visit to the Pacific Northwest](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-a-visit-to-the-pacific-northwest)
* Hard and soft 'g': [The Safety Rangers](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/decodable-the-safety-rangers), [Ginger and the Gerbil](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/decodable-ginger-the-gerbil)

### R-Controlled Vowels

* One-syllable words with r-controlled vowels: 'ar': [Living on the Farm](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-living-on-the-farm), [To the Farm](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/r-controlled-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-text-to-the-farm)
* One-syllable words with r-controlled vowels: 'or': [The Forts](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-forts), [Thor and Greg](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/r-controlled-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-text-thor-and-greg)
* One-syllable words with r-controlled vowels: 'ur': [Murl and the Robin](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-murl-and-the-robin)
* One-syllable words with all of the r-controlled vowels: ‘ur’, ‘ar’, ‘ir’, and ‘er’: [Checking on the Surf](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-checking-on-the-surf)
* Multisyllable words with r-controlled vowels: 'ar': [The Art Party in the Garden](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-art-party-in-the-garden)
* Multisyllable words with r-controlled vowels: 'or': [Stormy the Horse](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-stormy-the-horse)
* Multisyllable words with r-controlled vowels: ‘er’, ‘ir’, and 'ur': [Running Partners](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-running-partners), [A Girl Named Shirl](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/r-controlled-vowels-skill-explainer/decodable-text-a-girl-named-shirl)
* Multisyllable words with r-controlled vowels: ‘or’ and ‘er’: [Ports and Harbors](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-ports-and-harbors)

### Vowel Teams and Diphthongs (Vowel Digraphs)

* Long 'o' vowel teams: [The Yellow Boat](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-yellow-boat)
* Long 'e' vowel teams: [Seeking Nuts for Winter](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-seeking-nuts-for-winter)
* Long 'a' vowel teams: [Fay’s Birthday Party](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-fays-birthday-party)
* Long 'i' vowel teams: [Dinner by the Fire](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-dinner-by-the-fire)
* Long 'u' vowel teams: [Jeans for Pru](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-jeans-for-pru)
* Vowel teams 'oo', 'ew', 'ue', and 'ou': [The Field Trip to the Zoo](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-field-trip-to-the-zoo)
* Vowel team 'oo' as in *cook:* [Caleb’s Cookbook](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-calebs-cookbook)
* Vowel teams 'oo', 'ou', 'ew' and 'ue': [Youth Troop Soup](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-youth-troop-soup)
* Vowel team 'aw' as in *lawn* and 'au' as in *auto*: [The Jigsaw Puzzle](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-jigsaw-puzzle)
* Diphthongs 'oi' and 'oy': [Troy’s Pink Pig](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-troys-pink-pig)
* Diphthongs 'ou' and 'ow': [Rowdy on Broadway](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-rowdy-on-broadway)

See the [vowel teams and diphthongs skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/vowel-teams-and-diphthongs-skill-explainer/an-overview-of-vowel-teams-and-diphthongs) for more instructional resources.

### Trigraphs

* Trigraph ‘-tch’: [Pitch and Catch](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/trigraphs-tch-skill-explainer/decodable-pitch-and-catch)
* Trigraph ‘-dge’: [Mudge and the Fudge](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/trigraphs-dge-skill-explainer/decodable-mudge-and-the-fudge)

* Mixed digraphs and trigraphs: [The Fun Run](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/trigraphs-dge-skill-explainer/decodable-the-fun-run)

See the ['-tch' spelling rule skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/trigraphs-tch-skill-explainer/overview-of-the-tch-spelling-rule) and the ['-dge' spelling rule skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/phonics-patterns/trigraphs-dge-skill-explainer/overview-of-dge-spelling-rule) for more instructional resources.

### Review of Patterns Previously Taught

* FLoSS(Z), digraphs, trigraphs, and blends: [The Soft Doll](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/phonics-patterns/flossz-pattern-skill-explainer/decodable-the-soft-doll)

### Consonant ‘-le’

* Consonant ‘-le’: [The Apple Puzzle](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-apple-puzzle), [The Lambert Family Dinner](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-lambert-family-dinner)

### Silent Consonant Letters

* Silent consonants: [Chaos at the Castle Game](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-chaos-at-the-castle-game)

### Multisyllabic Words

* Two-syllable words with a closed syllable: [The Insect Mascot](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-insect-mascot), [The Junk Shop](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-junk-shop)
* Two-syllable words that end in a ‘y’ (representing the long ‘e’ sound): [A Picnic with Pals](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-a-picnic-with-pals)
* Two-syllable words with the schwa and closed-syllable pattern: [The Man with the Velvet Hat](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-man-with-the-velvet-hat), [The Red Robin Rocket](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/the-red-robin-rocket-schwa-decodable)

* Three-syllable words with short vowels and schwa: [The Tennis Match](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-tennis-match)
* One- and two-syllable words with open syllables: [The Paper Jet](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-paper-jet), [Watching the Buffalo and Elk](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-watching-the-buffalo-and-the-elk)

See the [multisyllabic skill explainer](https://readinguniverse.org/skill-explainer/multisyllable-words/multisyllabic-words-skill-explainer/an-overview-of-multisyllabic-words) for more instructional resources.

### Prefixes

* Prefixes 'un-', 're-', 'non-', and 'mis-': [The Big Test (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/decodable-the-big-test-reading-universe.pdf)
* Prefixes 're-': [Jade Remakes a Fort  (opens in new window)](https://files.readinguniverse.org/PDFs/decodable-jade-remakes-a-fort-reading-universe.pdf)

### Suffixes

* Suffixes ‘-s’ and ‘-es’: [Sack Lunches](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-sack-lunches)
* Adding the suffix ‘-s’: [Caps and Bags](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-caps-and-bags)

* Closed-syllable words with the suffix '-ing': [Running and Watching](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-running-and-watching)
* Closed-syllable words with the suffix ‘-ed’ as a sound: [Watching the Frog](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-watching-the-frog)
* Closed-syllable words with the suffix ‘-ed’ as a syllable: [Hiking to the Falls](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-hiking-to-the-falls)
* Closed-syllable words with suffixes: ‘-s,’ ‘-ed,’ ‘-ing’: [The Odd Plant](https://readinguniverse.org/resources/pdf/fluency/decodable-the-odd-plant)

# Lyrical Literacy

Lyrical Literacy: Why Singing Works—A Neuroscientific Exploration of Brain Research\*

## Mission Statement

**Lyrical Literacy is exercise for the brain.** "Use it or lose it" is the mantra of biological systems. Just as people who train only their upper body become injury-prone and physically imbalanced, the same principle applies to cognitive development. Despite its proven benefits, singing is often cut from school curricula. Through tongue twisters, lullabies, and nursery rhymes, we teach language by singing basic vocabulary and survival phrases, engaging multiple brain regions simultaneously to create balanced cognitive development.

## Abstract

**Lyrical Literacy:** Enhancing Cognitive Development through Music and AI. Humanitarians AI Incorporated supports the "Lyrical Literacy" project through both the Fellows Program and technical expertise to harness AI for promoting cognitive and language development through singing. We mentor emerging researchers and provide technical guidance to develop AI-powered tools, songbooks, and interactive platforms that encourage daily engagement with music. Our involvement focuses on leveraging AI to personalize song recommendations, analyze user engagement, and create accessible resources, including hundreds of public domain and simple songs available on SoundCloud. By integrating neuroscience research with AI, we help ensure that the project maximizes its impact on language acquisition, memory enhancement, and overall brain health for diverse populations.

## Project Overview

**Lyrical Literacy** is a pioneering initiative from Humanitarians AI that harnesses artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive and language development through music. This research-based program explores the powerful intersection of neuroscience, music, and education to create personalized learning experiences for diverse populations.

## Core Concept

At the heart of Lyrical Literacy is the understanding that music engages more brain regions simultaneously than almost any other human activity. By leveraging AI technologies to create customized songs, storybooks, and audiobooks, the project provides multimodal learning experiences that target specific cognitive and linguistic skills while maintaining high engagement levels.

## Key Components

1. **AI-Generated Musical Content**: Custom-created songs tailored to individual learning objectives, cultural contexts, and developmental needs
2. **Multimodal Learning Materials**: Interactive storybooks with accompanying musical elements and audiobooks that incorporate rhythmic and melodic components
3. **Personalization Engine**: AI algorithms that adapt content based on learning progress, preferences, and specific developmental goals
4. **Accessibility Focus**: Materials designed for diverse populations, including those with learning differences, language barriers, or neurodevelopmental conditions

## Campaign Themes

**"Brain Exercise Songs for Children"** - This campaign theme aligns with Lyrical Literacy's neuroscientific foundation. Your organization focuses on music as "exercise for the brain," leveraging research showing that singing engages multiple brain regions simultaneously. The campaign promotes educational songs specifically designed based on neuroscience principles to enhance cognitive development, language acquisition, memory formation, and overall brain health in children. These songs represent practical applications of your research into how music activates interconnected neural networks.

**"Create Your Own Educational Music"** - This campaign theme connects to your AI-powered approach to personalized learning. Humanitarians AI provides tools and resources for creating custom educational music using AI technologies like Suno and Udio. This reflects your organization's work in developing "AI-Generated Musical Content" and personalization engines that adapt content based on specific learning needs. This campaign helps others implement the research-backed techniques you've developed through your comprehensive studies on music's cognitive benefits.

## Research Framework

Lyrical Literacy employs a robust research methodology to track and analyze the impact of music-based interventions on:

* Phonological awareness and literacy development
* Second language acquisition and pronunciation
* Social-emotional skill development
* Executive function and attention regulation
* Memory formation and retention
* Neural plasticity across different age groups

## Applications

The project implements its approach across multiple contexts:

* **Educational Settings**: Supporting early literacy, multilingual classrooms, and special education
* **Therapeutic Environments**: Providing tools for speech therapists, psychologists, and occupational therapists
* **Home Learning**: Offering accessible resources for families to support cognitive development
* **Community Programs**: Implementing group-based musical learning in underserved communities

## Technology Platform

Humanitarians AI employs cutting-edge technology to power Lyrical Literacy:

* Natural language processing to generate contextually appropriate lyrics
* Music generation algorithms that create culturally relevant and age-appropriate melodies
* Voice synthesis technology that produces natural-sounding vocals with appropriate emotional expression
* Adaptive learning systems that track progress and adjust content difficulty

## Impact Measurement

The project maintains rigorous evaluation protocols, collecting both quantitative and qualitative data on:

* Cognitive assessment measures before and after interventions
* Neuroimaging studies documenting changes in neural activity and connectivity
* Educational outcomes including standardized test performance
* Qualitative feedback from educators, parents, and participants

Through this comprehensive approach, Lyrical Literacy aims to expand our understanding of music's role in cognitive development while creating accessible, engaging tools that support learning across diverse populations and contexts.

## Research Papers

<https://github.com/nikbearbrown/Lyrical-Literacy/tree/main/Research>

## 1. The Neuroscience of Singing: A Comprehensive Survey of Research and Applications

### Abstract

This comprehensive survey examines the neuroscientific evidence supporting the cognitive and developmental benefits of singing, with a focus on practical applications across educational, therapeutic, and organizational contexts. Drawing on decades of research, we explore how singing activates interconnected neural networks that enhance language processing, memory, attention, and social connection. The paper presents detailed case studies showcasing successful implementations in early childhood education, second language acquisition, therapeutic interventions for neurological conditions, and organizational team building. Findings demonstrate that singing represents a uniquely powerful cognitive activity that engages more brain regions than almost any other human behavior, making it an invaluable tool for cognitive enhancement across the lifespan.

## 2. Music Training and Mathematical Cognition: A Critical Analysis

### Abstract

This critical analysis examines the relationship between music training and mathematical cognition, investigating how musical experience might enhance various aspects of mathematical thinking. Research has explored connections between music and numerical representation, pattern recognition, spatial reasoning, and algebraic thinking. This report critically evaluates the evidence for these connections, assessing methodological strengths and limitations, exploring contradictory findings, and considering practical implications with attention to contextual factors.

## 3. The Harmonious Mind: A Comprehensive Survey of Music Training's Impact on Second Language Acquisition

### Abstract

This comprehensive survey examines the relationship between music training and second language acquisition, focusing specifically on pronunciation accuracy, phonological awareness, and auditory processing. Drawing on neurological research and classroom case studies, we explore the shared neural foundations between music and language processing and analyze how musical experience enhances language learning capabilities. The survey presents evidence from multiple educational contexts and age groups, demonstrating that musical training creates fundamental changes in auditory processing that transfer to language acquisition. Case studies from diverse educational settings illustrate successful implementation strategies while highlighting critical factors for effectiveness.

## 4. Music Engagement and Social-Emotional Learning Barriers: A Critical Analysis

### Abstract

This critical analysis examines the relationship between music engagement and social-emotional barriers to learning, investigating how musical experiences might address various challenges that impede learning. Research has explored music's impact on social anxiety, communication apprehension, self-efficacy deficits, and peer relationship difficulties. This report evaluates the evidence for these connections, assessing methodological strengths and limitations, exploring contradictory findings, and considering practical implications with attention to contextual factors.

## 5. Music Training and Second Language Pronunciation: A Critical Analysis

### Abstract

This critical analysis examines the relationship between music training and second language pronunciation, investigating how musical experience might enhance spoken aspects of language learning. Research has explored connections between music and pronunciation accuracy, phonological discrimination, and oral fluency. This report evaluates the evidence for these relationships, assessing methodological strengths and limitations, exploring contradictory findings, and considering practical implications with attention to contextual factors.

## 6. The Harmonious Brain: A Comprehensive Survey of Neural and Cognitive Effects of Musical Training and Singing

### Abstract

This comprehensive survey examines the profound influence of musical training and singing on neural architecture and cognitive function across the lifespan. Drawing on neuroimaging, behavioral, and longitudinal studies, we document the structural and functional brain changes associated with musical activities and explore their transfer effects to non-musical domains, particularly language processing and executive functions. The paper presents detailed case studies across diverse populations—from children with typical development to those with language disorders and adults with neurological conditions. Findings reveal that musical engagement induces significant neural adaptations and provides unique therapeutic pathways for various conditions.

## 7. The Role of Music in Enhancing Reading Comprehension and Retention: A Comprehensive Survey

### Abstract

This comprehensive survey examines the profound relationship between music and literacy, with particular emphasis on how musical interventions can enhance reading comprehension and memory retention. The integration of music into educational practices offers multisensory experiences that benefit all learners, with exceptional advantages for those with learning differences such as dyslexia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have further expanded possibilities for personalized music-based learning. This survey synthesizes current research, presents illustrative case studies, and offers practical recommendations for educators and researchers.

Phonological awareness (PA) is a multilevel, oral language skill typically defined as the sensi­ tivity to the sound (or phonological) structure of spoken words apart from their meanings. Phonological (linguistic) units in­ clude syllabic (words, syllables) and subsyllabic units (onsets and rimes, phonemes). Phonemic or phoneme-level awareness is the most complex level of phonological awareness because it requires the detec­ tion and manipulation of the smallest linguistic units: pho­ nemes. Initial phoneme-level skills include isolating, catego­ rizing, and blending phonemes to form words, whereas more advanced [...] Phonological awareness, particularly at the phoneme level, has a direct role in many components of literacy develop­ ment including decoding and spelling. There is a link between phoneme-level awareness and decoding and encoding in alpha­ betic writing systems because graphemes (letters) represent phonemes (sounds) in written words. That is, phoneme-level awareness, in conjunction with alphabet knowledge, enables children to understand how graphemes are mapped onto pho­ nemes and blended to form spoken words (Adams, 1990; Share, 1995). Additionally, PA has an indirect effect on reading com­ prehension because decoding skill is related to reading fluency which, in turn, aids comprehension (LaBerge & Samuels, 1974; Storch & Whitehurst, 2001). International Literacy Association | 2019 POSITION STATEMENT AND RESEARCH BRIEF Phonological Awareness in Early Childhood Literacy Development 2 Phoneme-level awareness is the most complex level of phonological awareness because it requires the detec­ tion and manipulation of the smallest linguistic units: pho­ nemes. The International Literacy Association maintains that phonological awareness has a critical role in early literacy and language development.
